items.title: Separate triplets from swing
items.summary: Dividing a quarter-note beat into three equal parts creates eighth-note triplets.
objectives: Switch between straight eighths, triplets and the study swing without changing the quarter-note pulse.

explanation: Dividing a quarter-note beat into three equal parts creates eighth-note triplets. Count one-trip-let, two-trip-let while the click stays on the beat. A common practice approximation for swung eighths uses the first and third of those three slots.
Real swing changes with tempo and style; a fixed two-to-one ratio is only a study model. Compare straight eighths, full triplets and a long-short pair on the same pitch before changing notes.
guided_steps: Clap three equal syllables per click.
Play full triplets on G.
Play the swing pattern and compare its long-short spacing with straight eighths.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating swing as a new time signature
common_mistakes.correction: Keep the meter and change subdivision placement.

content.reflection: What improved, what was still difficult, and what will you repeat next session?

completion_criteria: Switch between straight eighths, triplets and the study swing without changing the quarter-note pulse.
Explain the main idea in your own words and pass the knowledge check.

items.title: Place notes on a sixteenth-note grid
items.summary: Four equal sixteenth notes fit one quarter-note beat.
objectives: Repeat four bars of the sixteenth pattern with clear rests.

explanation: Four equal sixteenth notes fit one quarter-note beat. Count 1 e and a, then repeat for beats two, three and four. The hand may remain quiet on most slots while the internal count continues.
Begin at a slow tempo. Clap the first and last sixteenths of each beat, then play them on one pitch. Do not confuse a short note with a fast tempo: the quarter-note click remains your reference.
guided_steps: Speak all sixteen subdivisions in a bar.
Clap slots one and a of each beat.
Play the scored pattern, damping during rests.

common_mistakes.problem: Compressing the last subdivision before the next beat
common_mistakes.correction: Divide the beat equally and practise the a-to-one transition.

items.title: Use muted attacks as rhythm
items.summary: A ghost note is a muted percussive attack without a clearly sustained pitch.
objectives: Distinguish pitched notes, ghost attacks and silence in four clean loops.

explanation: A ghost note is a muted percussive attack without a clearly sustained pitch. Touch the string lightly with the fretting hand and pluck gently. Avoid touching only at a strong harmonic node if that creates an unwanted ringing tone.

Keep ghost attacks quieter than the main notes. They should support the rhythm, not obscure where the chord begins. First alternate a pitched note with a muted attack; then add rests so the three sounds remain distinct.
guided_steps: Alternate one fretted A and one muted attack.
Make a rest after each pair and compare all three sounds.
Play the ghost study quietly with the click.

common_mistakes.problem: Squeezing the muted string against the fret
common_mistakes.correction: Use damping contact without fretting a clear pitch.

items.title: Connect notes with hammer-ons, pull-offs and slides
items.summary: A hammer-on sounds a higher fretted note through the fretting hand after an initial pluck.
objectives: Demonstrate all three connections slowly with similar note volume.

explanation: A hammer-on sounds a higher fretted note through the fretting hand after an initial pluck. A pull-off releases a higher note to a lower note already prepared on the same string. A slide moves between frets while maintaining useful contact.

Work with two nearby notes and compare their volumes. Pull-offs need a controlled release, not a large sideways yank. For a slide, hear the destination before moving and arrive on its intended beat. Synth playback demonstrates timing and pitch, not the physical technique.
guided_steps: Pluck D at A-string fret five and hammer to E at seven.
Prepare D and release E into it for a pull-off.
Slide C to D on the A string, then compare all three approaches.

common_mistakes.problem: Using extra force to make the second note louder
common_mistakes.correction: Reduce the gap, prepare the destination and balance the first attack.

items.title: Hear and outline seventh chords
items.summary: Adding a seventh to a triad gives four chord tones.
objectives: Build and distinguish major7, dominant7 and minor7 on C.

explanation: Adding a seventh to a triad gives four chord tones. Cmaj7 is C–E–G–B, C7 is C–E–G–Bb, and Cm7 is C–Eb–G–Bb. Notice that major seven and dominant seven differ even though both have a major third.
Play the root, third, fifth and seventh separately. Compare one changed note at a time. A chord symbol is useful only when you connect it to a sound and a playable location.
guided_steps: Name and play the C7 arpeggio.
Change Bb to B and hear Cmaj7.
Change E to Eb with Bb retained and hear Cm7.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating every symbol containing 7 as the same chord
common_mistakes.correction: Read the quality and identify both third and seventh.

items.title: Move smoothly between chord tones
items.summary: Voice leading connects notes with purposeful movement.
objectives: Play and explain the C–B–A–F bass line under its slash chords.

explanation: Voice leading connects notes with purposeful movement. In a bass part, a nearby chord tone can create a smoother line than jumping to every new root in the same register. Keep the requested bass note when a slash chord specifies it.
Compare C–G/B–Am–F with C–G–Am–F. The first bass line descends C–B–A before moving to F. Smoothness is one option; roots and larger leaps may suit a different arrangement.
guided_steps: Locate C, B, A and F around the first five frets.
Play the slash progression one note per bar.
Compare it with the root-only version and describe the difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Choosing nearby notes without checking the chord
common_mistakes.correction: Confirm the note belongs to the intended harmony or written bass instruction.

items.title: Aim a passing note at a destination
items.summary: An approach note leads into an intended target, often a chord tone on the next strong beat.
objectives: Resolve four approaches to their planned chord roots on time.

explanation: An approach note leads into an intended target, often a chord tone on the next strong beat. A chromatic approach sits one semitone above or below that target. Its usefulness comes from the resolution, not from being in a scale shape.
Practise the arrival first. For C to D, try C then C# briefly before D. Over a different harmony that C# may be tense; keep it deliberate and short until your ear understands its effect.
guided_steps: Play the next chord root exactly on beat one.
Add one semitone-below approach on beat four of the previous bar.
Repeat the full C–Dm–G–C study without extending the fill.

common_mistakes.problem: Holding the approach instead of reaching the target
common_mistakes.correction: Shorten it and rehearse the next downbeat first.

items.title: Build a simple walking line
items.summary: A basic walk often places one note on each quarter beat.
objectives: Play the four-bar walk and explain the two chromatic approaches.

explanation: A basic walk often places one note on each quarter beat. Start by outlining the chord with roots, thirds and fifths; use a nearby approach to connect to the next chord. The exact note choice depends on the chart and style.

In the original C–Dm–G–C study, identify each bar before playing. C# leads to D and F# leads to G as brief approaches. Keep the pulse even and make the harmony clear before experimenting with more chromatic movement.
guided_steps: Play only the four roots for one chorus.
Name each chord tone in the written walking study.
Add the approach notes and record two uninterrupted loops.

common_mistakes.problem: Choosing four random scale notes for every bar
common_mistakes.correction: Plan strong chord tones and the arrival at the next change.

items.title: Change feel with repeated notes and octaves
items.summary: A rock or pop part may rely on repeated eighth notes, while a disco-inspired part often uses octave motion.
objectives: Play two contrasting textures with stable timing and quiet unused strings.

explanation: A rock or pop part may rely on repeated eighth notes, while a disco-inspired part often uses octave motion. These are starting textures, not complete definitions of genres. Note length and accents can change the feel without changing the pitches.
Play a short repeated-note groove and then an octave version. Keep both at the same tempo. Choose the version that fits the drum pattern and leaves the melody clear.
guided_steps: Play steady A eighths at a comfortable tempo.
Alternate low A and octave A with clean string skipping.
Try a sparse verse followed by an octave chorus.

common_mistakes.problem: Letting octave jumps increase the tempo
common_mistakes.correction: Keep the click fixed and shorten unnecessary movement.

items.title: Explore space in reggae and roots-based grooves
items.summary: Different arrangements distribute weight differently across a bar.
objectives: Maintain a spacious repeated groove for one minute without adding unplanned attacks.

explanation: Different arrangements distribute weight differently across a bar. A spacious reggae-inspired study can leave beat one silent while a country-inspired study alternates a root and fifth. These exercises illustrate choices; neither is a rule for every recording in that style.
Listen for where the drummer places weight, how long bass notes ring and how phrases repeat. Try one sparse pattern for a full minute before adding a fill. The empty space should feel intentional.
guided_steps: Count through the silent first beat of the scored study.
Keep the pitched notes full and the rests clear.
Compare with two half-note roots and fifths over the same pulse.

common_mistakes.problem: Filling every rest because the line feels empty
common_mistakes.correction: Repeat the sparse pattern until the space feels stable.

items.title: Learn a short phrase by ear
items.summary: Separate a phrase into rhythm, pitch contour and note locations.
objectives: Reconstruct a two-bar original phrase with its main pitches and rests.

explanation: Separate a phrase into rhythm, pitch contour and note locations. Listen to one or two bars, tap the rhythm, then find the first pitch with a reference. Work in small pieces instead of guessing through an entire song.

After finding the notes, compare durations and rests. Write your own tab only after you can sing or imagine the phrase. A lawful recording or the original ear-training examples can be repeated privately for this practice.
guided_steps: Listen to one short original motif without watching its notes.
Tap its rhythm and hum or imagine its contour.
Find the notes, reveal the score, and correct one detail.

common_mistakes.problem: Looking at tab before trying to hear the phrase
common_mistakes.correction: Delay the answer reveal until after a real listening attempt.

items.title: Perform a groove and explain your choices
items.summary: Choose one original progression and create an eight-bar part.
objectives: Deliver two coherent eight-bar takes with a reliable return after the variation.

explanation: Choose one original progression and create an eight-bar part. Include a stable main pattern, one intentional variation and a clear return. Use a fill only if you can land at the next section on time.

Listen back separately for time, note endings and harmonic clarity. Ask a bandmate or teacher for one practical observation when available. A recording is evidence of this performance, not a permanent label of your ability.
guided_steps: Choose a progression and write its eight-bar form.
Rehearse the main groove before adding one variation.
Record two takes and compare using the milestone checklist.

common_mistakes.problem: Judging a performance only by difficult techniques
common_mistakes.correction: Evaluate time, sound, harmony and recovery first.
